A decade ago, physicists using twin detectors in Washington State and Louisiana detected gravitational waves—subtle ripples in space-time—for the first time. The discovery confirmed Albert Einstein’s prediction of such waves. Gravitational waves are created whenever massive objects accelerate. In the first detections, pairs of black holes in our galaxy that had been orbiting each other eventually merged. Although gravity holds us down on Earth, it is actually very weak, so gravitational waves distort space only by a tiny amount. In the black hole mergers recorded in 2015 by LIGO, the passing waves caused the arms of the L-shaped detectors, each 2.5 miles long, to stretch and contract by less than the width of an atom. Physicists describe these as high-frequency, short-wavelength waves that jiggled the detectors for a few seconds, corresponding to the final death spiral of merging black holes.

Now, astronomers have recorded the faint background hum from a different kind of gravitational wave. These lower-frequency, longer-wavelength waves seem to come from every direction in the sky. While the LIGO detections involved collisions between black holes only a bit more massive than the sun, the waves producing this background hum are thought to arise from orbiting pairs of supermassive black holes millions of times more massive, scattered about the cosmos. Data also suggests the hum is slightly more intense in the Southern Hemisphere sky. This surprising asymmetry is one of several new puzzles for astronomers to investigate, hinting at uneven distributions of supermassive black hole pairs across the universe.

Theorists long suspected such a hum existed, but its evidence has taken years to amass. Radio telescopes called pulsar timing arrays finally recorded enough data to tease out the faint signal amid radio noise. These arrays combine signals from multiple radio telescopes worldwide, boosting overall sensitivity and allowing astronomers to isolate gravitational-wave signals more effectively. Scientists reported using the MeerKAT array in South Africa to track slight changes in the timing of radio waves from more than 80 pulsars—rapidly spinning neutron stars. As low-frequency gravitational waves drift by, the pulsars are nudged, altering their radio emissions by a tiny amount. Astronomers use these shifts to infer properties of the waves, which “stretch or contract the universe by around 20 meters or so.” Pulsars, located hundreds or even thousands of light-years away, serve as a vast detector—one far larger than humans could build. Earlier work had hinted at this hum after analyzing 15 years of pulsar data, but MeerKAT has achieved similar results in less than five years. “Because of the sensitivity [of MeerKAT] and the number of pulsars we can observe, we got a similar result in just four and a half years, which is really exciting,” says astrophysicist Matthew Miles.

Compared to the 2015 signals that lasted only seconds, these newly detected low-frequency waves have wavelengths of about a light-year. It takes about a year for two consecutive wave crests to pass, so scientists need several years of observations to be sure the signal is real. Another difference is that pairs of supermassive black holes responsible for these waves may orbit each other for thousands of years before merging, emitting low-frequency gravitational waves throughout that time.

In northern Bolivia, on the edge of the Amazon rainforest, lies a savannah called the Llanos de Moxos... Archaeologists once thought the Amazon basin’s soil would have been too poor to have sustained a large human population before Europeans arrived. Dr Lombardo is head of a team proving them wrong. The idea that the pre-Columbian Amazon was pristine has taken a nose-dive in recent years... Scientists have found several lines of evidence suggesting habitation, including once-populated sites and tree species that seem to have been transplanted. In a paper published recently, Dr Lombardo and his colleague provide evidence of large-scale hydrological engineering and maize-planting... The Llanos de Moxos is mostly flat, and is flooded for months each year. These are where trees grow, and where people dwelt—building with earth, for lack of stone.

Remnants of some of their earth-built structures can still be seen. One area in particular, the 4,500 sq km Monumental Mound Region, is home to hundreds of mounds, some more than 20 metres tall... The extent of the Casarabe’s earthworks suggests there were a lot of them. That raises the question of how they fed themselves. Using satellite images and LIDAR, Lombardo’s group has identified a system of canals and ponds near the mounds... They suggest the canals drained water from the savannah into the ponds during the rainy season, keeping parts of it dry enough to be farmed, and that this water was then used for irrigation during the dry season. They also searched local sediments for pollen and phytoliths... The pollen and the phytoliths suggested that the Casarabe grew maize, to the exclusion of almost anything else. How numerous the Casarabe were remains unclear... Estimating how much maize was produced—and the numbers this could have supported—will need further fieldwork.

As for the fate of the Casarabe people, many suspect they were ravaged by Old World diseases... Radiocarbon dating suggests people stopped living on at least some of the mounds around 1400, almost a century before Columbus’s landfall. But others remained, and were still cultivating maize as late as 1550. Stone axe heads, and jewellery made of copper and lapis lazuli, suggest commerce with the Andes... Diverse ways of burying the dead—some more opulent than others—imply a social hierarchy. The most colossal of the mounds might have carried specific religious significance... ...Most of the savannah is now owned by ranchers. The Sirionós—the indigenous people who live there today—have no connection to the Casarabe culture. Locals are aware of the remains, often building their homes on top of ancient mounds... Many report turning up ceramics and bones while farming. And they are curious to know more about the history of their lands.
passages.V3:
The premise of Albritton Jonsson and Wennerlind’s … Origins of Capitalism to the Climate Crisis is that contemporary economic life is dominated by “Neoclassical Scarcity.” This is an orthodox economic model, in which scarcity of goods leads to high prices, which spurs innovation to find new resources, substitutes, or production methods, which brings prices down. Paradoxically, the scarcity concept at the heart of modern economics is also the motor of material abundance. Such neoclassical economics ushered in a faith in market equilibriums (...). More fundamentally, it “assumed that people had an insatiable desire, not for any specific good, but for consumption in general.”

It is this assumption of consumerist scarcity that the authors want to denaturalize. While such an idea has, today, been enthroned as nearly indisputable, they show how it emerged out of cultural conditions: the explosion of consumer culture, bourgeois anxieties about labor unrest, and a view of the world as “stock” to be exploited. These conditions and assumptions need not guide our future. If you want to dethrone a concept, give it an embarrassing genealogy. For the authors, neoclassical scarcity originates from a tradition of “Cornucopian” thought, which emerged among early modern alchemists, speculators, millenarian Christians, and philosophers.

For these techno-optimists, nature was not the scanty, harsh provider. Rather, it “hath in its bowels an infinite, and inexhaustible treasure” waiting to be unearthed through land improvement and scientific experimentation. Some of these thinkers applied a violently patriarchal model to the task of discovery. For Francis Bacon, the “secrets of nature” were a feminine jewel to be wrested by the male scientist who must “conquer and subdue her [nature]”. Others emphasized harmony and alchemical balance. But for all of them, the improvement of nature meant one thing: “If the natural world was infinitely improvable, it followed that the need to limit desires was no longer pressing.” This belief in natural replenishment was exemplified by Nicholas Barbon, who happily observed that “Beasts of the earth, Fowls of the Air, and Fishes of the Sea, Naturally Increase. (…) And the Minerals of the Earth are Unexhaustible.” (...) In contemporary paeans to capitalist flourishing, we hear that “technology is a resource-liberating mechanism. It can make the once scarce now abundant.” Resources—meaning everything from honeybees to bauxite—just want to be free so they can serve us.

The point for the apostles of Abundance, as it was for Barbon, is that any gospel trying to curb materialist desire is both painful and unnecessary, a hairshirt for a world with nothing to repent. Even worse, to restrain desire would remove the incentive to tinker in workshops and laboratories to find new ways of unlocking resources. Learning to restrain desires in order to live within a finite, God-given world was once the aim of what Albritton Jonsson and Wennerlind call “Neo-Aristotelian Scarcity,” a conservative view of natural limits that emphasized hierarchy, prudence, a distaste for greed and gluttony, and a disapproval for using money to make more money. With the early modern Cornucopians, a new vision of ever-increasing riches—what we now know as 2 percent year-on-year GDP growth—was unleashed upon the world.
passages.V4:
Today, China, Russia, and the United States, to say nothing of the mid-level and smaller powers, are all running a strange simulation of the Weimar Republic: that weak and wobbly political organism that governed Germany for 15 years from the ashes of World War I to the ascension of Adolf Hitler. The entire world is one big Weimar now, connected enough for one part to mortally influence the other parts, yet not connected enough to be politically coherent. Like the various parts of the Weimar Republic, we find ourselves globally in an exceedingly fragile phase of technological and political transition. I see no Hitler in our midst, or even a totalitarian world state. But don’t assume the next phase of history will provide any relief to the present one. This is the usefulness of Weimar. What, exactly, was Weimar? The great German historian Golo Mann called it a sprawling and unwieldy ‘empire without an emperor.’ World War I ended in defeat, 1.75 million German military deaths, and almost a half-million German civilian deaths. The country was shattered, and Germany was on the verge of social chaos. It was in that context that leading German politicians and lawyers, meeting in the Thuringian town of Weimar, devised a new constitutional arrangement that sought to avoid the autocratic tendencies of Kaiser Wilhelm II and Otto von Bismarck before him.

But the new arrangement was just too weak to withstand the pressures of what was to come. Two-thirds of Germany was still called Prussia, governed under different rules than the other federal states. As for Bavaria, there was constant talk of separation from the Reich. If all this seems like a far more complicated version of the U.S. Constitution with its separation of powers and 50 states, it was—and it was made more unwieldy by economic and social anarchy. There was catastrophic inflation during the early Weimar years and catastrophic depression toward the end. Weimar’s ‘normal state was crisis,’ writes the late historian Gordon A. Craig. In that sense, Weimar was like our planet today: intimately connected, so as to have crises that cut across oceans. To recall Weimar is to emphasize our growing interdependencies and to accept moral responsibility for them. It wasn’t all doom and gloom: there were periods of economic growth, cultural blossoming, and political compromises under Gustav Stresemann.

But catastrophes like the Great Depression doomed the republic. History is Shakespearean as well as geopolitical: Weimar’s vacuum was eventually filled by Nazi totalitarianism. Our world today must have a different destiny. Weimar is now a permanent condition for us, as we are connected enough by globalization to affect each other intimately without having the possibility of true global governance. And that is not the worst outcome—since, had Hitler not arrived, Weimar might ultimately have righted itself. Geography is not disappearing. But it is shrinking. Digital technology makes different parts of the globe affect each other as intimately as Weimar’s states once did. Will this new global Weimar find stability, or suffer a cataclysmic fate? Truly, we are all trapped with each other.

Tribalism certainly functioned in the distant past as a survival strategy, with societies that had more fiercely loyal members likely to do better than those with freethinkers who threatened the group’s social cohesion. But does a preference for cognitive bias serve our needs any longer, especially when democratic processes allow us to hold onto our bias and still tolerate the divergent opinions of others - if we feel put out by others telling us what to do, we can always wait until the next election and vote them out of power. In other words, when we feel like we can be both tribal and loyal to our in-group and cooperate with those who we cast as outsiders, does this give us an edge that lets us live better lives with less stress?
opts: Tribalism once ensured social cohesion, but in democratic societies, cognitive bias persists despite mechanisms that allow cooperation and tolerance of differing views.
The survival benefits of tribalism are questionable in modern democracies, where individuals can balance group loyalty with cooperation, reducing conflict and stress.
Although tribalism was once crucial for survival, modern political structures may render it obsolete by fostering tolerance and reducing the risks of rigid group loyalty.
While tribalism historically enhanced group survival, modern democratic systems challenge its necessity by enabling both in-group loyalty and cooperation with outsiders.

There are several linguistic phenomena that, when examined closely, give evidence that people speak through characters, much like authors of literary works do, in everyday discourse. However, most approaches in linguistics and in the philosophy of language leave little theoretical room for the appearance of characters in discourse. In particular, there is no linguistic criterion found to date, which can mark precisely what stretch of discourse within an utterance belongs to a character, and to which character. And yet, without at least tentatively marking the division of labor between the different characters in an utterance, it is absolutely impossible to arrive at an acceptable interpretation of it. As an alternative, one may take character use seriously, as an essential feature of discourse in general, a feature speakers and listeners actively seek out in utterances.
opts: The presence of characters in discourse is a crucial but overlooked linguistic phenomenon, as current theories lack precise criteria for identifying character use in utterances.
While language theories have yet to establish criteria for character use in discourse, recognizing characters as central to discourse is key to accurate interpretation.
Everyday discourse involves characters much like literary works, yet linguistic theories have not fully accounted for how characters function within utterances.
Linguistic and philosophical theories struggle to define the role of characters in discourse, despite their essential presence in everyday speech.

The passage given below is followed by four alternate summaries. Choose the option that best captures the essence of the passage.

China's Chang'e 5 mission collected about 1.7 kilograms of rock and soil from Oceanus Procellarum in the north western corner of the moon's near side. Orbital imagery suggests the crust there formed about 1.5 billion years ago. But that relative youth is at odds with computer models, which show that a small body like the moon should by then have lost the internal heat remaining from its formation—heat needed to drive volcanic resurfacing and crust development. Lacking samples from this region, scientists had estimated its surface age by counting impact craters: older surfaces, they reasoned, would bear more such scars than younger ones would. This technique extends to any solid planetary body. Samples that U.S. and Soviet missions collected from the moon's equatorial, north eastern and northern regions between 1969 and 1976 indicate those surfaces are three billion to four billion years old. “The Apollo samples were like ground truth for the crater-counting models,” says Julie Stopar, a geomorphologist at the Lunar and Planetary Institute in Houston. But the earlier samples cover only those older regions: “Anything that happened between roughly three to one billion years ago, we didn't have samples of.”
opts: China's Chang’e 5 mission retrieved samples from a geologically young lunar region, challenging the crater-counting models used to estimate surface ages.
The Chang’e 5 mission’s lunar samples suggest a younger crust than earlier models predicted, raising questions about the moon’s internal heat and volcanic activity.
New samples from China’s Chang’e 5 mission challenge previous crater-counting estimates, highlighting gaps in our understanding of lunar surface evolution.
The moon’s relatively young crust, suggested by Chang’e 5 samples, contradicts earlier models and questions assumptions about the moon’s thermal history.
